eyebrow: Python for Data Science · Chapter 5, Lesson 26
subtitle: Turning silent data problems into loud, specific failures.

eyebrow: The practice data — five deliberate problems
caption: pandas enforces none of SQL's PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL, CHECK, or FOREIGN KEY — you write the checks yourself.

eyebrow: Five families of checks, one line each
code:
orders["order_id"].is_unique                               # False
orders["amount"].notna().all()                              # True
orders["amount"].between(0, 10000).all()                    # False
orders["status"].isin(["pending","shipped","delivered"]).all()  # True
orders["customer_id"].isin(customers["customer_id"]).all()  # False
caption: unique, complete, in-range, allowed values, related — the pandas equivalents of SQL's constraints.

eyebrow: See the offending rows, not just False
code:
orders[~orders["amount"].between(0, 10000)]
# order 5002: amount -15.0

orders[orders["order_id"].duplicated(keep=False)]
# both rows of order 5003
caption: Negate the check and use it as a filter — this is the output you hand to whoever owns the source system.

eyebrow: Bundle every rule into one function
caption: A named True/False Series — one place that holds every rule and evolves with the data.

code:
report = validate(orders, customers)
failed = report[~report].index.tolist()
assert not failed, f"Validation failed: {failed}"
# AssertionError: Validation failed: ['order_id is unique', ...]
caption: assert stops the notebook or script right there — bad data never flows into a model or a dashboard.
